title: Chocolate in Georgia? Ancient Pots Say Yes — 1,000 Years Ago!
summary:
Imagine biting into a chocolate bar. Now imagine that same treat reaching people in Georgia 1,000 years ago — long before any grocery store existed.

Scientists just found the earliest known traces of cacao east of the Mississippi River. They studied tiny pieces of ancient pottery found near the Etowah Indian Mounds in Georgia. The pots were used at a big feast about 1,000 years ago.

Cacao is the plant that gives us chocolate. It comes from Mesoamerica — warm, tropical places like southern Mexico. But Etowah is far from those places. So how did cacao get there?

Maybe travelers carried it. Maybe it was traded from person to person, like a relay race across the continent. Scientists aren't sure yet.

One cool clue: the cacao DNA on the pots was old and broken down — not fresh. That means it wasn't from a scientist eating a candy bar nearby! The team even got permission from the Muscogee people, who hold Etowah sacred, to study the pottery.

What does this tell us? The ancient Southeast wasn't isolated. People were connected through trade and travel. As archaeologist Adam King says, "The Indigenous world of the Southeast was an international world." Pretty amazing for 1,000 years ago!
why_it_matters: Learning that people traded and traveled long distances 1,000 years ago can change how you think in history class — the past was far more connected than it looks.

background_read: Chocolate comes from cacao, and long before candy bars existed, people in Mesoamerica (the warm region of southern Mexico and Central America) ground up cacao beans and drank them as a bitter, spicy drink.
Cacao was so valuable there that the beans were sometimes used like money.
Georgia is a U.S. state in the Southeast, and the Etowah Indian Mounds there are big earthen hills built long ago by Native Americans.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists studying tiny pieces of ancient pottery, with permission from the Muscogee people, plus archaeologist Adam King.
WHAT: They found the earliest known traces of cacao — the chocolate plant — east of the Mississippi River, used at a feast about 1,000 years ago.
WHERE: At the Etowah Indian Mounds in Georgia, far from cacao's home in Mesoamerica.
WHY: It shows the ancient Southeast was connected to faraway places through trade and travel, not isolated.

perspectives.description: Scientists say the pots prove the ancient Southeast was an 'international world' linked by trade with distant places.
The Muscogee hold Etowah sacred, so the team asked their permission before studying the pottery — a reminder that ancient sites belong to living communities too.
Nobody knows exactly how cacao traveled so far; it may have been passed from person to person like a relay race, and researchers are still trying to find out.
